image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Multi-series line chart.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Overlaid lines for many yearly series in a single panel  
- One series (2025) is highlighted in red, while the others are muted gray  
- No faceting, stacking, or small multiples

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Date within first half of year (Jan.–June) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage change in U.S. dollar index | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Year | Temporal / ordinal sequence | Separate line series; color emphasis (2025 in red, other years in gray) |
| 2025 annotation value (“2025 -10.7%”) | Quantitative + label | Text label attached to highlighted line endpoint |
| Endpoint marker for highlighted series | Quantitative (final value at end date) | Point marker on the red line’s last observation |

Hard to count the lines, but about 2/3 of the time the dollar rose, and 1/3 it declined. While the drop this year was the largest percentage decline since 1986 there is a limit what can be deduced from this. Observations? : I notice there is one squiggle line that’s highlighted red, which I am made to believe is the focal point of the distribution. The red line’s lowest point is around late April, and starting from mid to late January, the line experienced a trend of exponential decay. 
    Wonders? : The data’s caption indicates that the data is related to the worth of a dollar bill. I wonder why low currencies, like the dollar bill and 5 dollar bill are not as valuable anymore, and what factors contribute to that change. 
    How does this apply to your life? : This graph is relevant to me because I spend money on food and school supplies. It’s fascinating to put money into perspective from modern time to different times in history because it shows how the value of money has declined over time. For example, my sports medicine teacher buys a box of 16 medical tape rolls for $80, but she said it used to cost her about $30. So each tape today is $5, but “back then,” was $1.87. In present day, if she didn’t spend more on tape, she could only afford up to 6 rolls, which is 38% less tape. In the past, a $1.87 could get her single roll, but now, she can’t even afford to purchase one with that same amount. 
    Create a catchy title! : Is your $1 bill useless?

comments.raw_comment: When I look at this graph, I notice that the U.S. dollar dropped sharply in the first half of 2025 by 10.7%, which is the biggest decline compared to any other year since 1986. The red line representing 2025 clearly stands out from the gray lines of past years, most of which stayed closer to zero. This makes me wonder what caused such a dramatic drop.
